claim: Maternal smoking has been linked to pre-term delivery.
source: Maternal smoking has adverse effects on offspring health including pre-term delivery (Stock and Bauld, 2020; Liu et al., 2020), stillbirth (Marufu et al., 2015), and low birth weight (Ventura et al., 2003), and is associated with pregnancy complications such as maternal higher blood pressure, and gestational diabetes (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Stock and Bauld, 2020; Liu et al., 2020).

claim: Maternal smoking has been linked to stillbirth.
source: Maternal smoking has adverse effects on offspring health including pre-term delivery (Stock and Bauld, 2020; Liu et al., 2020), stillbirth (Marufu et al., 2015), and low birth weight (Ventura et al., 2003), and is associated with pregnancy complications such as maternal higher blood pressure, and gestational diabetes (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Marufu et al., 2015).

claim: Maternal smoking has been linked to low birth weight.
source: Maternal smoking has adverse effects on offspring health including pre-term delivery (Stock and Bauld, 2020; Liu et al., 2020), stillbirth (Marufu et al., 2015), and low birth weight (Ventura et al., 2003), and is associated with pregnancy complications such as maternal higher blood pressure, and gestational diabetes (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Ventura et al., 2003).

claim: Maternal smoking is associated with pregnancy complications such as maternal higher blood pressure.
source: Maternal smoking has adverse effects on offspring health including pre-term delivery (Stock and Bauld, 2020; Liu et al., 2020), stillbirth (Marufu et al., 2015), and low birth weight (Ventura et al., 2003), and is associated with pregnancy complications such as maternal higher blood pressure, and gestational diabetes (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).

claim: Maternal smoking is associated with gestational diabetes.
source: Maternal smoking has adverse effects on offspring health including pre-term delivery (Stock and Bauld, 2020; Liu et al., 2020), stillbirth (Marufu et al., 2015), and low birth weight (Ventura et al., 2003), and is associated with pregnancy complications such as maternal higher blood pressure, and gestational diabetes (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).

claim: Maternal smoking exposes the developing fetus to harmful chemicals in tobacco that negatively impact the health of newborns.
source: Consistent with the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) hypothesis, maternal smoking exposes the developing fetus to harmful chemicals in tobacco that negatively impact the health of newborns, resulting in early-onset metabolic diseases, such as childhood obesity (Montgomery and Ekbom, 2002; Toschke et al., 2002; Oken et al., 2008; Philips et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and reference to the DOHaD hypothesis.

claim: Maternal smoking results in early-onset metabolic diseases, such as childhood obesity.
source: Consistent with the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) hypothesis, maternal smoking exposes the developing fetus to harmful chemicals in tobacco that negatively impact the health of newborns, resulting in early-onset metabolic diseases, such as childhood obesity (Montgomery and Ekbom, 2002; Toschke et al., 2002; Oken et al., 2008; Philips et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Montgomery and Ekbom, 2002; Toschke et al., 2002; Oken et al., 2008; Philips et al., 2020).

claim: Self-reported smoking status is subject to underreporting among pregnant women.
source: Yet self-reported smoking status is subject to underreporting among pregnant women (England et al., 2007; Shipton et al., 2009; Salmasi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (England et al., 2007; Shipton et al., 2009; Salmasi et al., 2010).

claim: Underreporting of smoking could impact the effectiveness of interventions aimed at reducing smoking during pregnancy.
source: This could subsequently impact the effectiveness of interventions aimed at reducing smoking during pregnancy and may skew data on the risks associated with maternal smoking.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the underreporting problem.

claim: Underreporting of smoking may skew data on the risks associated with maternal smoking.
source: This could subsequently impact the effectiveness of interventions aimed at reducing smoking during pregnancy and may skew data on the risks associated with maternal smoking.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the underreporting problem.

claim: DNA methylation is one of the most commonly studied epigenetic mechanisms by which cells regulate gene expression.
source: DNA methylation is one of the most commonly studied epigenetic mechanisms by which cells regulate gene expression, and is increasingly recognized for its potential as a biomarker (Yousefi et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and a citation (Yousefi et al., 2022).

claim: DNA methylation is increasingly recognized for its potential as a biomarker.
source: DNA methylation is one of the most commonly studied epigenetic mechanisms by which cells regulate gene expression, and is increasingly recognized for its potential as a biomarker (Yousefi et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Yousefi et al., 2022).

claim: Differential DNA methylation has been established as a reliable biochemical response to cigarette smoking.
source: Differential DNA methylation has been established as a reliable biochemical response to cigarette smoking and was shown to capture the long-lasting effects of persistent smoking in ex-smokers (Shenker et al., 2013; Joehanes et al., 2016; Guida et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Shenker et al., 2013; Joehanes et al., 2016; Guida et al., 2015).

claim: Differential DNA methylation captures the long-lasting effects of persistent smoking in ex-smokers.
source: Differential DNA methylation has been established as a reliable biochemical response to cigarette smoking and was shown to capture the long-lasting effects of persistent smoking in ex-smokers (Shenker et al., 2013; Joehanes et al., 2016; Guida et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Shenker et al., 2013; Joehanes et al., 2016; Guida et al., 2015).

claim: Recent large epigenome-wide association studies have robustly identified differentially methylated CpG sites associated with adult smoking.
source: Recent large epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have robustly identified differentially methylated cytosine–phosphate–guanine (CpG) sites associated with adult smoking (Joehanes et al., 2016; Sikdar et al., 2019; Zeilinger et al., 2013) and maternal smoking (Joubert et al., 2016; Hannon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Joehanes et al., 2016; Sikdar et al., 2019; Zeilinger et al., 2013).

claim: Recent large epigenome-wide association studies have robustly identified differentially methylated CpG sites associated with maternal smoking.
source: Recent large epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have robustly identified differentially methylated cytosine–phosphate–guanine (CpG) sites associated with adult smoking (Joehanes et al., 2016; Sikdar et al., 2019; Zeilinger et al., 2013) and maternal smoking (Joubert et al., 2016; Hannon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Joubert et al., 2016; Hannon et al., 2019).

claim: Out of 290 CpG sites reported to be associated with maternal diabetes, pre-pregnancy BMI, diet during pregnancy, smoking, and gestational age, 19 sites were identified in more than one study and all of them associated with maternal smoking.
source: Our recent systematic review of 17 cord blood EWAS found that out of the 290 CpG sites reported to be associated with at least one of the following: maternal diabetes, pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), diet during pregnancy, smoking, and gestational age, 19 sites were identified in more than one study and all of them associated with maternal smoking (Akhabir et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a systematic review (Akhabir et al., 2022).

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms underlie associations between maternal smoking and birth weight in Europeans.
source: Furthermore, these findings have led to a more thorough investigation of the epigenetic mechanisms underlying associations between well-established epidemiological exposures and outcomes, such as the relationship between maternal smoking and birth weight in Europeans (Hannon et al., 2019; Witt et al., 2018; Küpers et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2021; Cardenas et al., 2019) and the less studied African American populations (Xu et al., 2021) as well as between maternal diet and cardiovascular health (Murray et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hannon et al., 2019; Witt et al., 2018; Küpers et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2021; Cardenas et al., 2019).

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms underlie associations between maternal smoking and birth weight in African American populations.
source: Furthermore, these findings have led to a more thorough investigation of the epigenetic mechanisms underlying associations between well-established epidemiological exposures and outcomes, such as the relationship between maternal smoking and birth weight in Europeans (Hannon et al., 2019; Witt et al., 2018; Küpers et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2021; Cardenas et al., 2019) and the less studied African American populations (Xu et al., 2021) as well as between maternal diet and cardiovascular health (Murray et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Xu et al., 2021).

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms underlie associations between maternal diet and cardiovascular health.
source: Furthermore, these findings have led to a more thorough investigation of the epigenetic mechanisms underlying associations between well-established epidemiological exposures and outcomes, such as the relationship between maternal smoking and birth weight in Europeans (Hannon et al., 2019; Witt et al., 2018; Küpers et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2021; Cardenas et al., 2019) and the less studied African American populations (Xu et al., 2021) as well as between maternal diet and cardiovascular health (Murray et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Murray et al., 2021).

claim: Only a handful of cohort studies were designed to assess the influence of maternal exposures on DNA methylation changes in non-Europeans.
source: Only a handful of cohort studies were designed to assess the influence of maternal exposures on DNA methylation changes in non-Europeans (Xu et al., 2021; Raynor and Born in Bradford Collaborative Group, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Xu et al., 2021; Raynor and Born in Bradford Collaborative Group, 2008).

claim: Systematic patterns of methylation, such as cell composition, could differ between individuals of different ancestral backgrounds.
source: It has been suggested that systematic patterns of methylation (Elliott et al., 2022), such as cell composition, could differ between individuals of different ancestral backgrounds, which could in turn confound the association between differential DNAm and smoking behaviors (Choquet et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Elliott et al., 2022; Choquet et al., 2021).

claim: Systematic differences in methylation patterns contribute to different smoking-related methylation signals at individual CpGs.
source: These systematic differences also contribute to different smoking-related methylation signals at individual CpGs (Elliott et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Elliott et al., 2014).

claim: A methylation score is usually tissue-specific and combines information from multiple CpGs using statistical models.
source: A methylation score is usually tissue-specific and combines information from multiple CpGs using statistical models (Yousefi et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Yousefi et al., 2022).

claim: Reducing the number of predictors and measurement noise in the data can lead to better statistical power and a more parsimonious instrument for subsequent analyses.
source: Reducing the number of predictors and measurement noise in the data can lead to better statistical power and a more parsimonious instrument for subsequent analyses.
evidence: The claim is based on established statistical knowledge.

claim: Almost none of the South Asian mothers were current smokers and had low smoking rates pre-pregnancy as compared to European mothers.
source: Notably, almost none of the South Asian mothers were current smokers and had low smoking rates pre-pregnancy as compared to European mothers, which is consistent with the broader trends of lower smoking rates in South Asian females (Reitsma et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Reitsma et al., 2021).

claim: Lower smoking rates in South Asian females is consistent with broader trends.
source: Notably, almost none of the South Asian mothers were current smokers and had low smoking rates pre-pregnancy as compared to European mothers, which is consistent with the broader trends of lower smoking rates in South Asian females (Reitsma et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Reitsma et al., 2021).

claim: The NutriGen Alliance is a consortium consisting of four prospective, population-based birth cohorts that enrolled birthing mother and newborn pairs in Canada.
source: The NutriGen Alliance is a consortium consisting of four prospective, population-based birth cohorts that enrolled birthing mother and newborn pairs in Canada. Details of these cohorts have been described elsewhere (de Souza et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (de Souza et al., 2016).

claim: The Illumina Human-Methylation450K BeadChip array covers CpGs in the entire genome.
source: About half of the START samples and selected samples from CHILD were hybridized to the Illumina Human-Methylation450K BeadChip (HM450K) array, which covers CpGs in the entire genome (Bibikova et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Bibikova et al., 2011).

claim: The GMEL customized array includes ~3000 CpG sites that were previously reported to associate with complex traits or exposures.
source: The GMEL customized array includes ~3000 CpG sites that were previously reported to associate with complex traits or exposures and was designed to maximize discovery while keeping the costs of profiling epigenome-wide DNA methylation down.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Cell-type proportions were estimated following a reference-based approach developed for cord blood.
source: Cell-type proportions (CD8T, CD4T, Natural Killer cells, B cells, monocytes, granulocytes, and nucleated red blood cells) were estimated following a reference-based approach developed for cord blood (Gervin et al., 2019) and using R packages 'FlowSorted.CordBloodCombined.450k' and 'FlowSorted.Blood.EPIC.'
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Gervin et al., 2019).

claim: The top associated CpGs with current maternal smoking were mapped to the GFI1 gene on chromosome 1, with cg12876356 as the lead.
source: The top associated CpGs with current maternal smoking were mapped to the growth factor independent 1 (GFI1) gene on chromosome 1, with cg12876356 as the lead (meta-analyzed effect = –1.11±0.22; meta-analyzed p=2.6 × 10–6; FDR adjusted p=0.006; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The meta-analyzed effect for cg12876356 was –1.11±0.22 with a p-value of 2.6 × 10–6 and FDR adjusted p-value of 0.006.
source: The top associated CpGs with current maternal smoking were mapped to the growth factor independent 1 (GFI1) gene on chromosome 1, with cg12876356 as the lead (meta-analyzed effect = –1.11±0.22; meta-analyzed p=2.6 × 10–6; FDR adjusted p=0.006; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The top associated CpG from the meta-analysis of smoking exposure was cpg01798813 on chromosome 17.
source: The top associated CpG from the meta-analysis of smoking exposure (hours per week) in the European-origin cohorts (Figure 2B) was cpg01798813 on chromosome 17, which was also associated with maternal smoking and was consistent in the direction of association (meta-analyzed effect = –0.18±0.04; meta-analyzed p=1.4 × 10–5; FDR adjusted p=0.04; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The meta-analyzed effect for cpg01798813 was –0.18±0.04 with a p-value of 1.4 × 10–5 and FDR adjusted p-value of 0.04.
source: The top associated CpG from the meta-analysis of smoking exposure (hours per week) in the European-origin cohorts (Figure 2B) was cpg01798813 on chromosome 17, which was also associated with maternal smoking and was consistent in the direction of association (meta-analyzed effect = –0.18±0.04; meta-analyzed p=1.4 × 10–5; FDR adjusted p=0.04; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The final MRSs included 15 and 143 CpG markers from the targeted array and the epigenome-wide HM450 array, respectively.
source: The final MRSs, validated using CHILD European samples (n=347), included 15 and 143 CpG markers (Supplementary file 1g) from the targeted array and the epigenome-wide HM450 array (Figure 1B), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the MRS construction presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both MRSs produced methylation scores that were significantly associated with maternal smoking history.
source: Both produced methylation scores that were significantly associated with maternal smoking history (ANOVA F-test p-values = 1.0 × 10–6 and 2.4×10–14 in CHILD and 3.6×10–16 and <2.2 × 10–16 in FAMILY; Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the best among alternative scores for CHILD and FAMILY (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the MRS validation presented in the manuscript.

claim: The epigenetic maternal smoking score was strongly associated with smoking status during pregnancy (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: [1.07,1.10], p=1.96 × 10–32) in the combined European cohorts.
source: As a result, the epigenetic maternal smoking score was strongly associated with smoking status during pregnancy (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: [1.07,1.10], p=1.96 × 10–32) in the combined European cohorts.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the association analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The maternal smoking MRS was significantly associated with increased number of hours exposed to smoking per week in the two White European cohorts (1.93±0.33 hr per 1 unit of increase in MRS, FDR adjusted p=1.2 × 10–7).
source: Meanwhile, the maternal smoking MRS was significantly associated with increased number of hours exposed to smoking per week in the two White European cohorts (1.93±0.33 hr per 1 unit of increase in MRS, FDR adjusted p=1.2 × 10–7; Supplementary file 1h; cohort-specific p=5.4 × 10–5 in CHILD and p=2.3 × 10–5 in FAMILY; Table 3), but not in the South Asian birth cohort (p=0.58; Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the association analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The maternal smoking MRS was not significantly associated with smoking exposure in the South Asian birth cohort (p=0.58).
source: Meanwhile, the maternal smoking MRS was significantly associated with increased number of hours exposed to smoking per week in the two White European cohorts (1.93±0.33 hr per 1 unit of increase in MRS, FDR adjusted p=1.2 × 10–7; Supplementary file 1h; cohort-specific p=5.4 × 10–5 in CHILD and p=2.3 × 10–5 in FAMILY; Table 3), but not in the South Asian birth cohort (p=0.58; Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the association analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A higher maternal smoking MRS was significantly associated with smaller birth size (–0.37±0.12, p=0.0023) in the South Asian cohort.
source: A higher maternal smoking MRS was significantly associated with smaller birth size (–0.37±0.12, p=0.0023; Table 3) and height at 1, 2, and 5- year visits in the South Asian cohort (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the association analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The MRS was associated with a smaller birth size (–0.22±0.07, p=0.0016; FDR adjusted p=0.019) in the combined European and South Asian cohorts.
source: We observed similar associations with body size in the White European cohorts (heterogeneity p-values >0.2), collectively, the MRS was associated with a smaller birth size (–0.22±0.07, p=0.0016; FDR adjusted p=0.019; Supplementary file 1h) in the combined European and South Asian cohorts.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: A higher maternal smoking MRS was associated with a lower birth weight (–0.043±0.013, p=0.001; FDR adjusted p=0.011) in the combined sample.
source: Meanwhile, a higher maternal smoking MRS was also associated with a lower birth weight (–0.043±0.013, p=0.001; FDR adjusted p=0.011; Supplementary file 1h) in the combined sample, though the effect was weaker in START (–0.03±0.02; p=0.094; Table 3) as compared to the White European cohorts.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EWAS results replicated the association between maternal smoking and CpGs in the GFI1 gene.
source: The EWAS results replicated the association between maternal smoking and CpGs in the GFI1 gene that is well described in the literature with respect to smoking (Joehanes et al., 2016; Sikdar et al., 2019), maternal smoking (Joubert et al., 2016; Hannon et al., 2019; Markunas et al., 2014; Richmond et al., 2015), and birth weight (Küpers et al., 2015).

claim: The association between maternal smoking and CpGs in the GFI1 gene is well described in the literature with respect to smoking.
source: The EWAS results replicated the association between maternal smoking and CpGs in the GFI1 gene that is well described in the literature with respect to smoking (Joehanes et al., 2016; Sikdar et al., 2019), maternal smoking (Joubert et al., 2016; Hannon et al., 2019; Markunas et al., 2014; Richmond et al., 2015), and birth weight (Küpers et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Joehanes et al., 2016; Sikdar et al., 2019).

claim: The association between maternal smoking and CpGs in the GFI1 gene is well described in the literature with respect to maternal smoking.
source: The EWAS results replicated the association between maternal smoking and CpGs in the GFI1 gene that is well described in the literature with respect to smoking (Joehanes et al., 2016; Sikdar et al., 2019), maternal smoking (Joubert et al., 2016; Hannon et al., 2019; Markunas et al., 2014; Richmond et al., 2015), and birth weight (Küpers et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Joubert et al., 2016; Hannon et al., 2019; Markunas et al., 2014; Richmond et al., 2015).

claim: The association between maternal smoking and CpGs in the GFI1 gene is well described in the literature with respect to birth weight.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Küpers et al., 2015).

claim: A weak dose-dependent relationship between the MRS and the four categories of maternal smoking status was present in CHILD but was not replicated in FAMILY.
source: A weak dose-dependent relationship between the MRS and the four categories of maternal smoking status in the severity of exposure ([0]=never smoked; [1]=quit before this pregnancy; [2]=quit during this pregnancy; [3]=currently smoking) was present in CHILD but was not replicated in FAMILY (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The AUC for detecting current smokers was 0.95 (95% confidence interval: 0.89–1) in CHILD.
source: The AUC for detecting current smokers were 0.95 (95% confidence interval: 0.89–1) and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.83–0.94) in CHILD and FAMILY (Figure 3), respectively, while the AUCs for detecting ever-smokers were 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54–0.67), 0.60 (95% CI: [0.55,0.69]; Supplementary file 1f), and 0.82 (95% CI: [0.55,1]; Figure 3), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The AUC for detecting current smokers was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.83–0.94) in FAMILY.
source: The AUC for detecting current smokers were 0.95 (95% confidence interval: 0.89–1) and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.83–0.94) in CHILD and FAMILY (Figure 3), respectively, while the AUCs for detecting ever-smokers were 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54–0.67), 0.60 (95% CI: [0.55,0.69]; Supplementary file 1f), and 0.82 (95% CI: [0.55,1]; Figure 3), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The maternal smoking MRS was consistently associated with increasing weekly smoking exposure in children reported by mothers at the 1 year visit (0.44±0.15, p=0.0044) in CHILD.
source: The maternal smoking MRS was consistently associated with increasing weekly smoking exposure in children reported by mothers at the 1 year visit (0.44±0.15, p=0.0044; Table 3) in CHILD, and at 3 year visit (0.86±0.26, p=0.0037; Table 3) in FAMILY, but not in START as all mothers reported non-exposure to smoking in children.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the association analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The maternal smoking MRS was consistently associated with increasing weekly smoking exposure in children at 3 year visit (0.86±0.26, p=0.0037) in FAMILY.

evidence: The claim is supported by data from the association analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The meta-analysis revealed no heterogeneity in the direction nor the effect size of associations for body size and weight between populations at birth or at later visits (heterogeneity p-values = 0.16–1).

claim: There was no evidence of the association between the MRS and any maternal outcomes.

evidence: The claim is supported by data from the association analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The significant association of the MRS with the newborn health metrics in START, in the absence of mothers' active smoking, could be the result of underreporting of smoking, poor recall of the time of quitting, and/or due to air pollution exposure.

claim: The cord blood DNAm signature of maternal smoking is perhaps not unique to cigarette smoking, but captures similar biochemical responses via the aryl hydrocarbon receptor.
source: This suggests that our cord blood DNAm signature of maternal smoking is perhaps not unique to cigarette smoking, but captures similar biochemical responses, for example, via the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (Vogel et al., 2020; Reynolds et al., 2015).

source: Firstly, cord blood provides a direct reflection of the in-utero environment and fetal exposure to maternal smoking.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cord blood.

claim: The use of MRS is a powerful tool to systematically investigate the influence of DNA methylation changes and whether it has lasting functional consequences on health outcomes.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study results.

claim: Epigenetic associations of maternal smoking are associated with newborn health.
source: Our results converge with previous findings that epigenetic associations of maternal smoking are associated with newborn health, and add to the small body of evidence that these relationships extend to non-European populations and that different ancestral populations can experience the early developmental periods differently.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and established knowledge.

claim: The relationships between epigenetic associations of maternal smoking and newborn health extend to non-European populations.
